nameStory: The harbour porpoise gets its name from its love of hanging out near harbors, coastal waters, and river mouths where boats come and go. Unlike their dolphin cousins who might venture far into the open ocean, these small marine mammals prefer to stay close to shore where the water is shallower and food is plentiful. Think of them as the 'homebodies' of the whale world!
description: The harbour porpoise is one of the smallest members of the whale family, measuring about the size of a large dolphin but with a more compact, rounded body. They have a distinctive triangular dorsal fin and a blunt, beakless face that gives them an almost puppy-like appearance. Their sleek bodies are dark gray to black on top with lighter gray sides, perfectly built for swift underwater hunting. These shy marine mammals are much smaller and more elusive than the dolphins most people picture.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Compact, torpedo-shaped body about 4-6 feet long with a distinctly rounded, blunt head that lacks the prominent beak of dolphins

idTips.label: Dorsal Fin
idTips.description: Small, triangular dorsal fin that's much more pointed and less curved than a dolphin's fin, often described as looking like a shark fin

idTips.label: Coloring
idTips.description: Dark charcoal gray to black back with lighter gray sides that fade to white on the belly, creating a subtle gradient effect

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Shy and quick-moving, often surfacing briefly with just a small splash before disappearing, unlike the playful jumping of dolphins

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found in shallow coastal waters, harbors, and river mouths rather than far offshore, often in waters less than 500 feet deep

habitat: In New England waters, harbour porpoises prefer shallow coastal areas, especially around bays, harbors, and the mouths of rivers like the Kennebec and Penobscot in Maine. They're most commonly spotted in waters less than 500 feet deep, often close enough to shore that you might see them from beaches or coastal trails. Look for them around underwater ledges and areas where cold currents bring up nutrient-rich water that attracts the small fish they love to eat.

seasonality.spring: Harbour porpoises begin returning to New England's warming coastal waters, often seen in small groups as they follow schools of herring and other fish inshore.
seasonality.summer: Peak viewing season when they're most active in shallow bays and harbors, often coming close to shore to feed on abundant fish populations.
seasonality.fall: Still commonly seen as they build up fat reserves before winter, though they may begin moving to slightly deeper waters as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Less frequently spotted from shore as they move to deeper offshore waters, though some individuals may remain in protected bays and harbors year-round.

funFact: Harbour porpoises have been found swimming hundreds of miles up rivers, sometimes appearing in completely landlocked areas where people never expect to see a whale - imagine the surprise of spotting one of these ocean animals in what looks like a freshwater lake!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with dolphins, but remember that porpoises have blunt, rounded heads without beaks, while dolphins have prominent bottle-like snouts. Porpoises also have small triangular fins versus dolphins' larger curved fins, and porpoises are much shyer - if you see playful jumping and acrobatics, it's probably a dolphin!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'porpoises,' these animals are actually small whales in the scientific sense - all dolphins, porpoises, and whales belong to the same group called cetaceans. The word 'porpoise' comes from old French meaning 'pig fish,' referring to their rounded, somewhat pig-like faces when viewed head-on.
compareHints: The harbour porpoise is the only true porpoise species regularly seen in New England waters, making it unique among local marine mammals. While dolphins in the area have prominent beaks and larger size, harbour porpoises maintain their distinctive blunt-headed profile and compact build. They're much smaller and more secretive than any of the dolphin species that visit New England, preferring quick, subtle surfacing over the dramatic breaching displays of their larger cousins.
